name: Uruguay
traditionNote: A classical Latin American civil-law system on the Spanish-French model, with codes at its centre and no doctrine of binding precedent: a Supreme Court ruling that a statute is unconstitutional applies only to the parties who obtained it.
summary: A statute (ley) is passed by both chambers of the Asamblea General — the Cámara de Representantes and the Cámara de Senadores — promulgated by the President with a minister, and published in the Diario Oficial, which is what makes it enforceable; the Civil Code sets the default at ten days after publication in the capital and longer elsewhere unless the statute fixes its own date. Decrees (decreto) are issued by the President in Council of Ministers and resolutions by ministries, and they too are published in the Diario Oficial. Since 1 July 2016 the Diario Oficial has been entirely digital, replacing the printed edition, and is free to read from midnight with no account or password. Constitutional review is concentrated and unusually narrow: only the Suprema Corte de Justicia may declare a statute unconstitutional, by action, exception or referral, and its ruling has effect only in the case in which it was given — the provision stays on the books for everyone else. Administrative acts are annulled not by the ordinary courts but by the Tribunal de lo Contencioso Administrativo, a separate body outside the judiciary.
hierarchy: Constitución de la República (1967, with the reforms of 1989, 1994, 1996 and 2004)
Treaties approved by statute, which enter the internal order at the rank of the approving statute
Ley — statutes of the Asamblea General, including the codes and the leyes de urgente consideración
Decretos del Poder Ejecutivo — decrees in Council of Ministers, and reglamentos executing the statutes
Resoluciones ministeriales and the acts of the descentralised bodies and autonomous entities
Decretos de las Juntas Departamentales — departmental decrees with the force of law in the department
Resoluciones de las Intendencias — departmental executive acts and municipal decisions

gazette.name: Diario Oficial
gazette.native: Diario Oficial de la República Oriental del Uruguay
gazette.authority: Dirección Nacional de Impresiones y Publicaciones Oficiales (IMPO), Centro de Información Oficial
gazette.coverage: Published every working day; entirely digital since 1 July 2016, when the printed edition was discontinued, with the archive of earlier issues alongside it
gazette.desc: The publication that makes a Uruguayan norm enforceable. IMPO states the terms plainly: the day's content is available from midnight, free, without registration or passwords, from any device, and the digital edition carries the same legal validity the printed one did.
gazette.howto: Open the day's issue and move through it by Sección, Índice, Documentos and Avisos, or download the whole issue as a PDF; earlier issues are reached by date. For the consolidated text of a norm rather than the day it appeared, cross to the Centro de Información Oficial's normative database.
gazette.note: Publication in the Diario Oficial is what starts the clock: the Civil Code default is ten days after publication in the capital, and further out in the interior, unless the norm fixes its own date.

constitution.name: Constitucion de la Republica
constitution.native: Constitución de la República Oriental del Uruguay
constitution.authority: IMPO — Centro de Información Oficial, maintaining the updated text
constitution.coverage: The 1967 text as amended by the plebiscitary reforms of 1989, 1994, 1996 and 2004; IMPO marks the page 'Documento Actualizado'
constitution.desc: A long constitution with an unusual amendment culture: it is changed by plebiscite, and Uruguayans reject far more amendments than they approve — pension, water and security reforms have all been decided at the ballot box. Article 332 is characteristic, providing that rights are not left unenforceable merely because the implementing statute has not been passed.
constitution.howto: Read the text section by section on IMPO; each article carries notes cross-referring to the articles and norms that bear on it. Reform can proceed by popular initiative, by a constitutional statute or by a constituent convention, and always ends in a plebiscite.
constitution.note: Only the Suprema Corte de Justicia can hold a statute unconstitutional, and its ruling binds only the case at hand; the provision remains in force for everyone else.

sources.name: Centro de Informacion Oficial (IMPO)
sources.native: Normativa y Avisos Legales — Centro de Información Oficial
sources.authority: IMPO, Dirección Nacional de Impresiones y Publicaciones Oficiales
sources.coverage: Statutes, decrees and resolutions, kept as updated texts with the amendments incorporated, alongside the constitution and the codes
sources.desc: The state's normative database, run by the same body that publishes the gazette — so the consolidated text and the published text come from one source rather than two. Norms are addressed predictably: a statute sits at /bases/leyes/<number>-<year>, so law 18.331 of 2008 is /bases/leyes/18331-2008.
sources.howto: Search by number and year, by keyword or by subject; an updated norm is marked 'Documento Actualizado' and each article carries notes to the norms that amended or interpreted it. The full text of the day's gazette remains the record of what was published.
sources.note: The updated texts are prepared by IMPO from the published items. Where the wording is contested, the Diario Oficial item is the record.

sources.name: Registro Nacional de Leyes y Decretos
sources.native: Registro Nacional de Leyes y Decretos
sources.en: National Register of Laws and Decrees
sources.coverage: The annual register of statutes and decrees, running back through the twentieth century, alongside the institutional databases IMPO maintains for particular bodies
sources.desc: The chronological record of what was enacted, kept separately from the day-by-day gazette. It is the reference for older norms, where a citation gives a year and a number but no publication date.
sources.howto: Work from the year and the number of the statute or decree; the institutional databases in the same section hold the normative collections IMPO maintains for individual public bodies, which is where some agency regulation is easiest to find.

sources.name: Parlamento del Uruguay
sources.native: Parlamento del Uruguay — Documentos y Leyes
sources.authority: Poder Legislativo — Cámara de Representantes and Cámara de Senadores
sources.coverage: Statutes by number and year, bills with their file histories, committee records, the Diario de Sesiones of both chambers, and the texts of ratified treaties
sources.desc: The legislature's own database, and the better route when you need the file behind a statute rather than its text: the exposición de motivos accompanying a bill, the committee's report and the debate in each chamber.
sources.howto: Search statutes by number or subject, or open a bill's ficha to see every document and date in its passage. Note that Uruguay's ley de urgente consideración has forced deadlines — if the chambers do not decide in time, the bill is deemed approved — so the dates in a file can matter as much as the votes.
sources.note: The site answers automated requests with 403 while serving browsers normally.

sources.name: Base de Jurisprudencia Nacional
sources.coverage: Judgments of the Suprema Corte de Justicia, the appellate courts and the lower courts, published by the judiciary and searchable by court, matter and date
sources.desc: The judiciary's free case-law database and the only public route to Uruguayan judgments. It matters most for constitutional questions: since a declaration of unconstitutionality binds only the case that produced it, what you are looking for is the line of rulings rather than a single decisive one.
sources.howto: Search by court, subject, date range or the norm applied; results give the judgment with its number and date. Rulings on unconstitutionality come from the Suprema Corte alone, so filter to it when that is the question.
sources.note: Coverage is uneven at the lower levels, and there is no official reports series that competes with it.

sources.name: Poder Judicial
sources.authority: Suprema Corte de Justicia and the courts under it
sources.coverage: Court structure and rules, acordadas of the Suprema Corte, case-tracking services, hearing lists and statistics
sources.desc: The judiciary's own site. The acordadas of the Suprema Corte are worth knowing about: they are the Court's general regulatory instruments for the functioning of the courts, and they govern procedure in ways a statute reader would not expect.
sources.howto: Take the acordadas for the Court's own regulations, and the consulta de expedientes services for tracking a case; judgments themselves are in the national case-law database.
sources.note: Administrative acts of the state are annulled by the Tribunal de lo Contencioso Administrativo, which sits outside this judiciary and whose site is frequently unreachable from abroad.

sources.name: gub.uy
sources.authority: AGESIC, for the whole central administration
sources.coverage: Every ministry and agency on one domain, with their resolutions, regulatory material, consultations and procedures
sources.desc: Uruguay put the entire central state on a single domain, which makes agency-level regulation unusually findable: a ministry's resolutions, guidance and public consultations are at a predictable address rather than on a site of its own design.
sources.howto: Go to the responsible body's section and look for its normativa or resoluciones; the same portal carries the trámites, which often state the operative rules more clearly than the norms behind them.
sources.note: A portal, not a gazette. A resolution takes effect through its publication or notification under the rules that apply to it, not by appearing here.

sources.name: Normativa departamental (Montevideo)
sources.authority: Intendencia de Montevideo and Junta Departamental de Montevideo
sources.coverage: The departmental digest — decrees of the Junta Departamental and resolutions of the Intendencia — consolidated by volume and subject
sources.desc: Shown as the pattern for Uruguay's nineteen departments. A decreto of a Junta Departamental has the force of law within the department, which makes departmental law a genuine second layer rather than mere administration, and Montevideo's digest is the most developed of the nineteen.
sources.howto: Browse the digest by volume and subject or search by number and year; resolutions of the Intendencia are indexed separately from the Junta's decrees. Other departments publish through their own Intendencia sites, with much less consolidation.
sources.note: Departmental norms are not in the national database. If a rule applies only in one department, the national sources will not have it.

sources.name: Ministerio de Relaciones Exteriores
sources.coverage: Treaty information, the status of agreements and the ministry's own normative material
sources.desc: Uruguay approves a treaty by statute and publishes both the approving statute and the treaty text in the Diario Oficial, so the treaty enters the internal order with the rank of that statute. This is the route to the diplomatic status of an agreement — signature, ratification, entry into force — which the gazette does not track.
sources.howto: Use the ministry's section for the status of agreements, then find the approving ley by number in IMPO or the parliamentary database; the text published with it is the operative one domestically.
sources.note: Mercosur instruments have their own incorporation route and may require an internal norm before they apply.

sources.name: AGESIC
sources.native: Agencia de Gobierno Electrónico y Sociedad de la Información
sources.coverage: Regulatory guidance and standards on data protection, access to public information, digital signature and interoperability, with the decisions of the data protection and transparency units
sources.desc: The body behind Uruguay's digital state, and the regulator whose material you need for data protection and access to information — two fields where the operative rules are in AGESIC's guidance and unit decisions rather than only in the statutes.
sources.howto: Look for the unit responsible — the Unidad Reguladora y de Control de Datos Personales, or the Unidad de Acceso a la Información Pública — and read its dictámenes and guidance alongside the statutes and decrees they interpret.
sources.note: Guidance and regulator practice, not legislation, though some of it is issued as binding decisions.

sources.name: Lenguaje Ciudadano (IMPO)
sources.coverage: Plain-language accounts of statutes and decrees of general interest, published alongside the norms themselves
sources.desc: An unusual thing for a gazette publisher to do: IMPO writes and publishes plain-language explanations of the norms it publishes, aimed at the people the rules apply to rather than at lawyers.
sources.howto: Browse by subject or search for the norm; each entry links back to the official text, which is the one that governs.
sources.note: Explanations, not law. Where the plain-language version and the norm differ, the norm governs.

sources.name: Mercosur
sources.authority: Secretaría del MERCOSUR, whose seat is in Montevideo
sources.coverage: The founding treaties and protocols, and the decisions, resolutions and directives of the bloc's organs, with their incorporation status for each member state
sources.desc: Uruguay is a founding member and hosts the Secretariat. Mercosur norms are not directly applicable the way EU regulations are: most require incorporation into national law by each member, and the bloc's own database records for each norm whether Uruguay has incorporated it and by which instrument.
sources.howto: Find the norm by organ, year and number in the normative database, then check its incorporation status for Uruguay and follow to the Uruguayan decree or statute that incorporated it — that instrument is what binds domestically.
sources.note: The site answers automated requests with 403 while serving browsers normally. Disputes go to the ad hoc arbitral tribunals and the Tribunal Permanente de Revisión, not to a standing court with direct effect.

sources.name: Tribunal de Cuentas
sources.native: Tribunal de Cuentas de la República
sources.authority: Tribunal de Cuentas de la República, a constitutional body
sources.coverage: Rulings and observations on public spending and contracts, ordinances on public accounting, and its opinions on departmental budgets
sources.desc: A constitutional body that audits the whole state and whose observaciones on a payment or a contract have real consequences: an act observed by the Tribunal can only proceed if the body reiterates the spending under its own responsibility, and that reiteration is itself published.
sources.howto: Search the rulings and ordinances by year and body; its opinions on the departmental budgets are the most detailed published account of departmental finance.
sources.note: The site answers automated requests with 401 while serving browsers normally.

findLaw.task: Find the current text of a statute
findLaw.steps: Open the norm in IMPO's normative database — a statute resolves at /bases/leyes/<number>-<year>, as in 18331-2008 — and check that it is marked 'Documento Actualizado'. The notes on each article point to the norms that amended or interpreted it.

findLaw.task: Read what was published on the day
findLaw.steps: Open the Diario Oficial for that date and work through Sección, Índice and Documentos, or download the issue as a PDF. This is the record of publication, and the date it gives is what the entry-into-force period runs from.

findLaw.task: Work out when a rule starts to apply
findLaw.steps: Read the final articles of the norm for its own date. If it fixes none, the Civil Code default applies: ten days after publication in the capital, and later in the interior — so a norm published today may bind in Montevideo before it binds elsewhere.

Search the national case-law database by court, subject or the norm applied. For constitutionality, filter to the Suprema Corte de Justicia and read the line of rulings rather than one: a declaration of unconstitutionality applies only to the case in which it was made.

findLaw.task: Follow a bill, or read why a statute was passed
findLaw.steps: Open the bill's file on the parliamentary site for the exposición de motivos, the committee reports and the debates in both chambers. Where the bill was declared of urgent consideration, watch the deadlines — the constitution deems such a bill approved if the chambers do not resolve it in time.

Identify the department, then its digest: for Montevideo, the departmental normative database holds the Junta's decrees and the Intendencia's resolutions, consolidated by subject. Departmental decrees have the force of law inside the department and appear in no national database.

findLaw.task: Challenge or check an administrative act
findLaw.steps: Annulment of an administrative act is not a matter for the ordinary courts: it goes to the Tribunal de lo Contencioso Administrativo after the administrative remedies have been exhausted. Start from the norms and the procedure on the state portal, and note that damages against the state are a separate claim in the ordinary courts.
findLaw.source: gub.uy / Tribunal de lo Contencioso Administrativo

subnational: Uruguay is a unitary state with a real second layer. Its nineteen departments each have an elected Junta Departamental, whose decretos have the force of law within the department, and an Intendencia that executes them — a structure closer to a legislature than to municipal administration, and one whose output is not collected nationally. Montevideo maintains the most developed digest of departmental norms; the other eighteen publish through their own Intendencia sites with far less consolidation, and older departmental decrees can be hard to obtain at all. Below the departments sit the municipios created by the 2009 decentralisation act, with elected local councils and limited powers. The Diario Oficial publishes national norms; departmental ones are published departmentally, so a search that stops at IMPO will miss anything that applies in only one department.
caveats: Uruguay's constitutional review is narrower than it looks: only the Suprema Corte can declare a statute unconstitutional, and the declaration has effect only in the case in which it was given, so a provision repeatedly held unconstitutional remains in force and must be challenged again by the next litigant. Administrative acts are annulled by a separate tribunal outside the judiciary, whose site is often unreachable from abroad. IMPO's updated texts are prepared from the published items and are the practical source, but the Diario Oficial item is the record; the entry-into-force default under the Civil Code differs between the capital and the interior. Departmental law is a genuine second layer and is published departmentally, not nationally. Case-law coverage is uneven below the Supreme Court, and there is no official reports series to fall back on. Nothing here is translated: Uruguayan law exists in Spanish only, and no state body publishes an English version of the constitution or the codes.
